Tech Report: A New Framework for Evaluating Voice Agents (EVA)

📅 24 Mar 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1715 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that conversational voice agents present a distinct evaluation challenge: they must simultaneously satisfy two objectives — accuracy (completing the user's task correctly and faithfully) and conversational experience (doing so naturally, concisely, and in a way appropriate for spoken interaction).
  • Sources indicate that we introduce EVA, an end-to-end evaluation framework for conversational voice agents that evaluates complete, multi-turn spoken conversations using a realistic bot-to-bot architecture.
  • We also provide benchmark results for 20 cascade and audio-native systems, such as speech-to-speech (S2S) models and Large Audio Language Models (LALMs).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that conversational voice agents present a distinct evaluation challenge: they must simultaneously satisfy two objectives — accuracy (completing the user's task correctly and faithfully) and conversational experience (doing so naturally, concisely, and in a way appropriate for spoken interaction). These objectives are deeply intertwined: mishearing a confirmation code renders perfect LLM reasoning meaningless, a wall of options overwhelms a caller who can't skim spoken output, and delayed responses can pass every accuracy check while remaining unusable in practice. Existing frameworks treat these as separate concerns — evaluating task success or conversational dynamics, but not both.

Sources indicate that we introduce EVA, an end-to-end evaluation framework for conversational voice agents that evaluates complete, multi-turn spoken conversations using a realistic bot-to-bot architecture. EVA produces two high-level scores, EVA-A (Accuracy) and EVA-X (Experience), and is designed to surface failures along each dimension. EVA is the first to jointly score task success and conversational experience. We release EVA with an initial airline dataset of 50 scenarios covering flight rebooking, cancellation handling, vouchers, and more — the first in a planned series of domains.

We also provide benchmark results for 20 cascade and audio-native systems, such as speech-to-speech (S2S) models and Large Audio Language Models (LALMs). Our biggest finding is that there is a consistent Accuracy-Experience tradeoff; agents that perform well on task completion tend to deliver worse user experiences, and vice versa.

The field presently lacks a framework that evaluates the full quality of voice agent interactions, as most existing efforts assess individual components in isolation. For example, AudioBench, SD-Eval, VoxEval, Kimi-Audio-Evalkit, VoiceBench and VoxDialogue evaluate core speech understanding capabilities for Speech-to-Text (STT) — transcription, paralinguistics, acoustic cues — but remain confined to single-turn, non-interactive settings. On the other hand, EmergentTTS-Eval and SHEET assess perceived speech quality using subjective listening tests (e.g., Mean Opinion Score). Beyond speech perception, FD-Bench, Talking Turns, Full-Duplex-Bench provide deeper analyses of conversational dynamics — interruptions, backchanneling, turn-taking — yet evaluate these in isolation from task-oriented tool use, leaving the relationship between dialogue quality and agentic capability unexamined. More recent efforts, notably VoiceAgentBench and CAVA, take steps towards evaluating the agentic capabilities of commercial voice agent systems, including tool-calling and complex instruction-following. However, these voice-agentic capabilities are not evaluated within complete conversational workflows that voice agents must navigate in practice: from initial user request through multi-step tool orchestration to final task resolution.

According to recent reports, the lack of frameworks that jointly capture accuracy and experience underscores the need for a framework that treats voice agent quality as an integrated whole. This means evaluating not only whether the task succeeded, but whether the agent communicated accurately, concisely, and naturally throughout, and surfacing how these dimensions trade off against one another in realistic deployment conditions.

End-to-end evaluation reveals interaction dynamics that are not apparent at the component level: whether the agent interrupts consumers during natural pauses in speech, whether it recovers smoothly when a user corrects a transcription error, or whether high latency disrupts the conversational flow enough to prompt users to repeat themselves or abandon the task entirely.

EVA simulates multi-turn spoken conversations over live audio in which the agent must invoke appropriate tools, adhere to task-specific policies, and reach a deterministically verifiable end state. EVA evaluates voice agents using a bot-to-bot audio architecture composed of five core components:.

Recent findings suggest that user Simulator — A conversational AI configured with a specific goal and persona that plays the role of a caller. It operates in audio using high-quality Text-to-Speech (TTS) models, ensuring the evaluation captures representative speech-understanding challenges in natural-sounding conversational speech and realistic turn-taking dynamics.

Voice Agent — The voice agent being evaluated, built with Pipecat, an open-source Python framework for real-time voice applications. EVA supports both cascade architectures (STT → LLM → TTS) and audio-native models (S2S or LALM → TTS).

Tool Executor — The engine that provides deterministic, reproducible tool responses via custom Python functions. It dynamically queries and modifies a predefined per-scenario database.

Validators — A set of validation metrics that check that conversations are complete and that the user faithfully reproduced the intended behavior and speech, with no human annotation required. Any conversation that fails in this validation step is regenerated, ensuring that only valid, correctly executed conversations enter evaluation. This stands in contrast to approaches that rely on post-hoc human labeling to identify simulator errors.

Metrics Suite — A suite of metrics evaluates the voice agent using the conversation recording, transcript, and tool call logs.

Each test case (scenario) in our framework is an evaluation record, structured to make tests reproducible:.

In a recent development, we release EVA with a synthetic airline dataset of 50 scenarios and 15 tools, spanning IRROPS rebooking, voluntary itinerary changes, cancellations, same-day standby, and compensation vouchers. Scenarios are designed to test temporal reasoning, policy-following, constraint satisfaction, and named-entity handling.

Sources indicate that EVA evaluates voice agents across two fundamental dimensions, EVA-A for accuracy, and EVA-X for experience. EVA also includes a set of diagnostic metrics. Unlike the primary metrics, these are not used directly to compare or rank models — rather, they offer granular insight into why a model scores the way it does, helping identify and understand specific failure modes (e.g., ASR, speech synthesis, etc.). We report pass@k (the probability that at least one of k runs succeeds) and pass^k (the probability that all k runs succeed) across three trials per scenario (k = 3), capturing both peak performance and behavioral consistency.

Industry observers note that EVA uses two evaluation methods: deterministic code-based metrics, which compute scores directly from structured data and are fast; and LLM-as-Judge metrics, which use Large Language Models (LLMs) to assess qualitative aspects of the conversation, or Large Audio Language Models (LALM) to evaluate speech directly. Each judge-based metric uses the model that performs best on a curated evaluation dataset for that specific metric.

In a recent development, task completion alone is a necessary but insufficient measure of accuracy. An agent can reach the correct end state while fabricating a policy detail, misreading a confirmation code aloud, or hallucinating a flight number mid-conversation. These failures are invisible to a binary pass/fail check but directly harm customers. EVA-A therefore measures three dimensions of accuracy:.

Industry observers note that turn-taking timing matters, but it tells only part of the story. An agent can have perfect timing while overwhelming a caller with a wall of spoken options they cannot skim, or repeatedly asking for information already given. These failures degrade the experience without ever involving a mistimed response. EVA-X therefore measures three dimensions of experience:.

We evaluated 20 systems — proprietary and open-source, cascade and audio-native — and find a consistent accuracy-experience tradeoff: agents that perform well on task completion tend to deliver worse user experiences, and vice versa — a tradeoff invisible to benchmarks that score only task completion. No single configuration dominates both axes, confirming that accuracy and experience must be measured jointly.

Additionally, we identified named entity transcription as a dominant failure mode. A single misheard character can cascade into an authentication failure and a full conversation breakdown. Also, multi-step workflows break agents in predictable ways. Rebooking a flight while preserving ancillary services — seats, baggage — is the dominant complexity breaker across all configurations. Finally, we observed that additional calibration is needed for real-world use cases. The gap between pass@3 and pass^3 is substantial across all configurations. Even agents that can complete a task often cannot do so consistently, which is critical for real-world success.

EVA is designed to provide rigorous, end-to-end evaluation of conversational voice agents, but several limitations are important to acknowledge, across the framework, data, and metrics dimensions:.

It has been revealed that metrics — LLM-as-judge models carry inherent biases and may favor certain response styles independent of quality, with additional risk of systematic bias when the evaluated and judge models share a provider. While we validate our judges against labeled datasets and report accuracy measurements on our website, these alignment scores do not eliminate systematic bias entirely. Additionally, task completion is measured as binary, which does not capture partial credits and may understate the relative quality of systems that fail gracefully versus catastrophically.

Simulation — The current release covers 50 English-language scenarios in a single domain (airline); results may not generalize to other domains, languages, or accents. Also, the user simulator may not perfectly replicate real caller behavior (e.g., disfluencies, hesitations, emotions) or guarantee full policy adherence.

Industry observers note that framework — The user simulator relies on a single commercial provider whose voice characteristics may systematically favor certain ASR systems, and the bot-to-bot pipeline — including audio format conversions and real-time audio interfaces — may not fully represent production deployments. Also, full reproduction requires commercial API access, and latency measurements will vary across providers and infrastructure.

On the evaluation side, we initiative to add prosodic quality assessment (pronunciation, rhythm, expressiveness) — presently an open problem after finding very low alignment between LALM-as-Judge and human judgments. We also plan robustness testing under noisy conditions, diverse accents, multilingual users, and varied speaker behaviors, alongside affect-aware evaluation of how agents respond to user distress. In terms of data, we are developing additional domain datasets — each with distinct policy structures, named entity profiles, and conversational dynamics — and more complex scenarios involving compound requests, multi-step follow-ups, and longer conversational memory. On the tooling front, we will release a results and error analysis application that automatically identifies errors per metric and model, surfaces representative examples for exploration, and generates structured summaries of each model’s strengths and weaknesses. Finally, we intend to expand the leaderboard continuously to provide an up-to-date assessment of voice agent capabilities across the field.

View more details about limitations and our upcoming roadmap here.

Core contributors include Tara Bogavelli, Gabrielle Gauthier Melançon, Katrina Stankiewicz, Oluwanifemi Bamgbose, Hoang Nguyen, Raghav Mehndiratta, and Hari Subramani.

According to recent reports, we also thank Lindsay Brin, Akshay Kalkunte, Joseph Marinier, Jishnu Nair, and Aman Tiwari for their careful data review and thoughtful contributions to the framework, and Fanny Riols, Anil Madamala, Sridhar Nemala, and Srinivas Sunkara for their management, leadership, and support throughout. We also extend our thanks to the PAVA and CLAE ServiceNow teams, whose prior work on evaluations and voice agents provided valuable inspiration for this project.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Motorola has kicked off its Android 17 rollout for the Razr Fold, marking the first major update for the organization’s first book-style foldable, and the start of a potentially interest 7 years of software support.

It has been revealed that the Motorola Razr Fold launched with Android 16 back in May 2026, and it remains a really good option for those looking to pick up a book-style foldable in the US. On top of solid specs across the board, it also carries the promise of 7 years of software support, something that few other Moto devices can tout.

But nowhere was it promises that Motorola would speed things up at all. A little over 3 months after Motorola announced the update and several weeks after other Motorola devices were updated to Android 17, the Motorola Razr Fold is finally getting its own Android 17 update.

Rolling out now, Android 17 for the Razr Fold is a 4.15GB~ update that appears to be available at least somewhat broadly. Reports are popping up on Reddit including one report from the EU (Hungary, specifically), with another user apparently in a Spanish-speaking region also seeing the update.

Sources indicate that we’re still waiting to see if the upgrade is available in the US (there’s a backlog of updates on our unit), but it’s certainly an update to look forward to. Apparently, Motorola finally fixed a weird UI issue that affected the Telegram app, something we ran into when using the device earlier this year.

Industry observers note that it’s great to see the upgrade out, but it’s noteworthy that Motorola is not setting a particularly encouraging precedent here. Razr Fold is one of the firm’s first devices to be promised 7 years of OS updates and software support, and its flagship-tier status certainly would have most expecting it to be updated ahead of some of Motorola’s more affordable, lower-tier devices that were updated over a month ago. Whatever the case, hopefully Motorola will speed things up over the next few years, especially with its $1,600 flagship Signature 27 on the horizon with the same software promises.

💡 Key Takeaways

Industry observers note that PENN Entertainment's online segment grew revenue in the third quarter, but the gain came from passed-through partner gaming taxes, not from players. The segment now needs a positive fourth quarter to reach a full-year target that has already been lowered.

Industry observers note that other revenues carried the whole of the Interactive segment’s third-quarter gain at PENN Entertainment. Segment revenue rose to $348.4 million from $297.7 million, while the third-party partner gaming-tax amounts booked there climbed to $191.4 million from $139.5 million a year earlier. Online gaming revenue itself fell 2.1% to $126.6 million from $129.3 million, as iCasino growth was offset by lower sports betting handle.

This pattern places PENN within the slowing-iGaming-growth story running through this week’s US operator reports.

According to recent reports, the nine-month figures show the same reliance on the gross-up. Interactive revenue reached $1,056.0 million, up from $903.9 million. The tax gross-up within it rose to $562.7 million from $405.6 million.

The group as a whole had a stronger quarter. Total revenue was $1,840.0 million. Net income came in at $32.6 million, against a $865.1 million net loss a year earlier. PENN also raised its full-year retail guidance to $5.89 billion in revenue and $1.973 billion in adjusted EBITDAR, increases of $16 million and $10 million.

Industry observers note that profitability is improving faster than revenue. The Interactive adjusted EBITDA loss for the first nine months shrank to $38.7 million from $227.6 million. PENN attributes that mainly to lower marketing, general and administrative, and labor costs.

Industry observers note that expansion has weighed on the quarter. PENN launched theScore Bet, theScore Casino and standalone Hollywood iCasino apps in Alberta on July 13, 2026. Excluding that third-quarter launch investment, Interactive adjusted EBITDA improved quarter over quarter throughout 2026, management said on the earnings call.

The standalone Hollywood iCasino brand is central to the plan. It posted record quarterly revenue in the second quarter. PENN is now leaning on its US growth, and on steady trends through October, to support the full-year Interactive target. That makes the brand a test for whether a mid-tier US online casino can turn profitable.

Sources indicate that the target itself has moved. In February, PENN guided the segment to breakeven adjusted EBITDA for 2026, which it described as a $268 million improvement from 2025. The cost of the Alberta launch is now built into a weaker outlook.

PENN Entertainment CEO Jay Snowden discussed the potential of more Canadian provinces launching iGaming on an earnings call today.

Sources indicate that the online segment still has to deliver. Reaching the revised target depends on Interactive turning its third-quarter loss into positive adjusted EBITDA in the fourth quarter.

Tech Report: TRL v1.0: Post-Training Library Built to Move with the Field

📅 31 Mar 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2223 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that we’re releasing TRL v1.0, and it marks a real shift in what TRL is.
  • It has been revealed that TRL now implements more than 75 post-training methods.
  • In a recent development, TRL is built for a field that doesn’t sit still.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we’re releasing TRL v1.0, and it marks a real shift in what TRL is. What started as a research codebase has become a dependable library people build on, with clearer expectations around stability. This isn't just a version bump. It reflects the reality that TRL now powers production systems, and embraces that responsibility.

It has been revealed that TRL now implements more than 75 post-training methods. But coverage isn’t the goal by itself. What matters is making these methods easy to try, compare, and actually use in practice. The design of the library wasn’t decided upfront. It is the result of years of iteration — the first commit goes back more than six years — and it has been shaped by everything the field threw at it: newly introduced algorithms, new models, shifting paradigms. Over time, this pressure forced the codebase toward a very specific design. Parts of it might look unusual at first, but like in many evolutionary codebases, they exist for a reason.

In a recent development, TRL is built for a field that doesn’t sit still. So the question is not how to design the perfect abstraction. It is how to make stable software in a domain that keeps invalidating its own assumptions. This is what we tried to solve in TRL v1.0, and this post explains how.

Sources indicate that post-training has not evolved as a smooth refinement of one recipe. It has moved through successive centers of gravity, each changing not just the objective, but the shape of the stack.

PPO [Schulman et al., (2017); Ziegler et al., (2019)] made one architecture look canonical: a policy, a reference model, a learned reward model, sampled rollouts, and an RL loop.

Then DPO-style methods such as the original DPO [Rafailov et al., (2023)], ORPO [Hong et al., (2024)], and KTO [Ethayarajh et al., (2024)] cut through that stack: preference optimization could work without a separate reward model, value model, or any online RL. Components that had looked fundamental suddenly looked optional.

According to recent reports, RLVR-style methods such as GRPO [Shao et al., (2024)] shifted the center again. On tasks like math, code, and tool use, rewards often come from verifiers or deterministic checks rather than learned reward models. Sampling and rollouts matter again, but the objects in the loop are no longer quite the ones PPO libraries were designed around.

Recent findings suggest that the lesson is not just that methods change. The definition of the core keeps changing with them. Strong assumptions here have a short half-life. This is probably why no post-training library is really stable yet.

So what does it mean to build a library for a field that won't sit still? The answer is counterintuitive: don't try to capture the essence of what's stable today. Instead, design around what could change. Reward models illustrate why: they looked essential in PPO, became optional in DPO, and came back as verifiers in RLVR methods — structures that could be deterministic functions rather than learned models. Any abstraction built around their original form would have been obsolete twice over by now. The library survives by recognizing that strong assumptions have a short life, and by making that changeability central to how the codebase is organized.

In a recent development, this is the environment in which TRL is downloaded 3 million times a month, and in which major downstream projects treat it as stable infrastructure. The field keeps shifting the ground, and at the same time, those users need things not to break.

Sources indicate that TRL didn’t make a deliberate decision to become a library. It found out it already was one. Projects like Unsloth and Axolotl — with thousands of consumers between them — had built directly on top of TRL’s trainers and APIs. A breaking change in TRL propagated instantly into their stacks. A renamed argument, a shifted default, a restructured output — any of these became someone else’s incident. The shift had already happened. v1.0 is the moment TRL acknowledged it explicitly.

It has been revealed that the unusual thing about TRL’s stability model is not what it guarantees, it is what it tolerates alongside those guarantees. Stable and experimental coexist within the same package, with explicitly different contracts. The stable core follows semantic versioning. The experimental layer makes no such promises — it is where new methods land while they are still being evaluated, and where the API can move fast to keep up with the field.

According to recent reports, this isn’t a compromise. It’s a response to a specific constraint: the field produces fresh methods faster than any of them can earn stability. Refusing to add immature methods would make TRL irrelevant within months. Adding them all to stable would break every downstream project every time an algorithm turned out not to work as expected.

Industry observers note that promotion from experimental to stable isn’t automatic. What matters is the ratio between maintenance cost and actual usage. Some methods earn their place because the community uses them heavily. Others become viable because we can make them cheap enough to maintain — and the design of the codebase is what makes that possible.

In practice, the stable surface includes trainers for SFT, DPO, Reward modeling, RLOO, and GRPO, along with their close variants. The experimental surface is broader and moves faster; for an up-to-date view, the best reference is the TRL documentation.

The breaking changes needed to reach v1.0 were distributed deliberately across the 0.x releases. Migration from the last 0.x version is minimal — see the migration guide.

In a domain where patterns keep changing, the temptation is to build flexible abstractions that can accommodate anything. Our answer was the opposite: limit abstractions to the strict minimum — while recognizing that this “minimum” is almost always overestimated.

In practice, this translates into a very local approach to code:.

Recent findings suggest that the goal is not to eliminate structure altogether — shared utilities still exist — but to avoid imposing abstractions where the domain itself is not yet stable. For instance, rather than defining a common base class for offline trainers, we prefer independent implementations when their future evolution is uncertain.

Judges are a good example of what happens when we don’t follow this principle. Early on, we introduced a Judge abstraction to unify the various ways of evaluating model outputs. It looked reasonable at the time. In practice, it was never really used — the abstraction didn’t match how people actually approached evaluation, and it added indirection without adding value. It still lives in the repo, mostly as legacy. In hindsight, shipping the concrete implementations without the unifying abstraction would have served users better.

This approach favors explicit and modifiable usage over rigid frameworks: less magic, but more control. It comes with an obvious cost: code duplication. While often seen as an anti-pattern, in this context it has proven not only acceptable, but effective. Contrary to intuition, it remains manageable in practice with a small but consistent discipline: keeping deltas between implementations minimal and avoiding unnecessary divergence. Like in the Transformers design philosophy, we accept duplication and local explicitness by design. The motivations largely coincide, with some nuance in focus.

Recent findings suggest that this is easier to see than to describe. Compare RLOO and GRPO: large parts of their implementation are duplicated almost line for line. That is not accidental, and it is not dead weight. These methods are close enough that keeping their code paths aligned makes them easier to read, easier to evolve, and cheaper to maintain.

Sources indicate that the goal of this comparison is not to argue that TRL should be judged as best on every axis. It should not. Some systems are built for maximum throughput (like PipelineRL), some are optimized for a narrower slice of the problem (like LLaMA-Factory), and some offer a more opinionated development experience in a specific environment (like Tinker). TRL occupies a different place in the ecosystem: it is a general-purpose post-training library that tries to keep the API and the code as simple as the domain allows, while combining broad method coverage, deep Hugging Face integration, a relatively low infrastructure burden, and an explicit stability contract.

Libraries like Unsloth and Axolotl are not included here because they build on top of TRL rather than sitting beside it in the comparison; in that sense, many of their users are also TRL users indirectly.

Some rows are factual (GitHub stars, Last release, Last commit), others are qualitative judgments (Semver stability).

Recent findings suggest that taken together, these comparisons point to a clear role for TRL: a general-purpose library designed to keep breadth, simplicity, integration, and stability in the same place. Its full downstream footprint is hard to measure, since most deployments are private and reverse dependencies are largely invisible, but the available signals already show that TRL operates at a distinctly different scale.

According to recent reports, by now, the logic of v1.0 should be clear: it is not a claim that post-training has stabilized. On the contrary, it is an acknowledgment that the field will keep shifting, and that we're confident that the library has the right shape to absorb whatever comes next. The question is not what comes after v1.0, but what’s next for v1.0.

Recent findings suggest that today, GRPO in TRL is primarily used through a synchronous loop: generate rollouts, score them, then step the optimizer. That shape is simple and dependable, but it ties throughput to the slowest stage and leaves performance on the table at scale.

According to recent reports, the fix is conceptually simple: generation and training don't need to be lock-stepped. We already have an early asynchronous GRPO design, and the next step is to harden it. The core idea is to decouple generation and training, letting generation run continuously on dedicated inference resources while training consumes a steady stream of scored trajectories, with buffering, backpressure, and clear policy-version accounting. This improves utilization and scales across GPUs and nodes. Other libraries already offer forms of asynchronous RL, but bringing it to TRL would make this style of training available through broader integrations, simpler APIs, and a much lower barrier to adoption.

The next candidates include KTO and newer distillation trainers such as SDFT, SDPO, and possibly GOLD or GKD. As discussed in Section 2, before moving them to stable, the goal is to minimize code differences across implementations and monitor sustained community interest relative to maintenance cost.

In a recent development, TRL supports large-scale training, including multi-node runs and larger models; the next step is to make this path significantly more robust and easier to operate in production. That includes stronger guarantees around distributed stability, clearer scaling defaults, and deeper support for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE), especially expert parallelism, where routing, load balancing, and memory behavior become critical.

Training is still too often driven by vibes. Loss curves go down, reward curves go up, a few samples look better than before, and people convince themselves the run is working. When it fails, they scroll through logs, compare runs by eye, and guess. That is already a weak interface for humans. For agents, it is worse: it is barely an interface at all.

One of the most vital directions for TRL is to make training legible to software, not just to people. That means going beyond dashboards and raw metrics to produce explicit signals: is the policy improving, collapsing, over-optimizing the verifier, drifting off-distribution, or plateauing? The goal is for TRL to surface these patterns automatically, explain them clearly, and turn them into actions.

The plan is to embed heuristics directly into the training loop and emit structured, actionable warnings — the kind a beginner can act on immediately and an agent can parse:.

In a recent development, not just logging what happened — reasoning about what it means and what to do next. Useful for beginners who need guardrails, and for agents that need a training stack they can actually automate.

Sources indicate that post-training doesn't converge. It shifts, and the next shift is already coming.

In a recent development, v1.0 is not a claim that things have settled. It's an acknowledgment that they haven't yet, and a commitment that the library can be relied on anyway. Six years of evolving alongside the field — and alongside the hundreds of contributors who made it possible — shaped a design we're confident is ready for what comes next, whatever that turns out to be. The community and the downstream projects had already assumed that stability — v1.0 makes it real.

Migration from the last 0.x release is minimal, and the migration guide covers everything. If you're newly introduced, now is a good time to start.

It has been revealed that both systems captured something useful. The problem is that neither record explains how the two interactions belong together.

In a recent development, A unified tracking pipeline gives forms and calls a common event format, preserves their acquisition context, and connects them to CRM outcomes. It also needs to survive a less tidy reality: repeated callbacks, missing campaign data, delayed updates, and a CRM that occasionally refuses requests.

Industry observers note that this tutorial builds the core of that pipeline with JavaScript and PostgreSQL. We will capture campaign parameters, define a shared event contract, and persist events alongside the work needed to deliver them. Provider authentication and CRM requests belong in adapters around this core, using the documentation for the services you choose.

Before writing an endpoint, decide what you are counting. A phone call can produce several status callbacks. A person can submit two forms. An existing customer can contact sales about a new purchase.

Use separate identifiers for these different things:.

This separation prevents two common mistakes. Deduplicating by call ID alone can discard later status updates. Counting every callback as a lead inflates demand.

For this implementation, each event is unique within a tenant and source. A tenant is the business whose data you are processing; the source identifies a website or provider account. The same provider event ID can therefore appear in two accounts without causing a collision.

It has been revealed that keep the original interactions even after you connect them to one contact. The form and the call are both useful evidence. Your reporting layer decides whether they represent one opportunity.

It has been revealed that campaign parameters are easiest to capture when the visitor first arrives. Waiting until the form submission can lose them if the visitor has already moved to another page.

It has been revealed that google's campaign URL documentation explains the roles of utm_source, utm_medium, and utm_campaign. The following helper reads those fields and a few optional ones, without copying the entire query string:.

Industry observers note that the browser's URLSearchParams interface handles query parsing and decoding. It saves you from writing string-splitting code that breaks on encoded characters.

According to recent reports, run this helper through your site's existing consent and attribution flow. Where storage is permitted, associate the result with an opaque attribution reference in your backend and retain that reference through the visit. A later form submission sends the reference; the server resolves it within the correct tenant and visitor session. The form must still work when attribution storage is unavailable.

According to recent reports, keep first-touch and current-touch records separately if you need both. Overwriting the first campaign every time someone returns makes the eventual report answer a different question.

Treat campaign labels as untrusted input. Visitors can edit query strings and hidden fields. Validate them on the server, escape them when displayed, and never use them as authorization or as the sole evidence for commission payments. Avoid putting names, email addresses, or other personal information in UTM values.

In a recent development, missing tags also need careful handling. An empty UTM object only tells you that no accepted UTM values were captured. Classifying a visit as direct, organic, or referral requires additional evidence and an explicit attribution rule.

Industry observers note that forms carry browser context naturally. Phone calls need a bridge between the number dialed and the marketing interaction that prompted the call.

There are two useful levels of precision. A number assigned to one campaign can identify that campaign. Dynamic number insertion can support a more detailed association by displaying tracking numbers according to a visitor or session mapping. That association depends on the provider's number allocation and expiry rules.

Recent findings suggest that providers differ in how they implement this, and in what they expose beyond it, such as keyword-level reporting or conversation analysis. If you are still choosing one, this comparison of attribution software with call tracking is a useful starting point. At the integration boundary, check which event identifiers, attribution fields, delivery mechanisms, and authentication options your configured product exposes.

Recent findings suggest that keep that provider-specific work in an adapter. Its job is to turn an authenticated notification into your event contract and resolve any attribution reference supported by the provider's data. The application schema below is an internal contract; each provider adapter translates its documented payload into that contract.

Store the basis of a match with the attribution record. For example, session_match, campaign_number, and unknown make different levels of evidence visible to reporting. If a number has been reassigned, use the mapping valid when the call occurred, not whichever mapping happens to be current when the callback arrives. If the evidence is ambiguous, leave the association unresolved.

Sources indicate that caller ID is a separate matter. A shared office number, a withheld number, or an outdated contact record can make automatic identity matching unreliable. A confirmed CRM contact ID or an authenticated account provides a stronger link. Treat a matching phone number as a candidate for reconciliation rather than proof that two records belong to the same person.

A shared event envelope lets the rest of your application work with a small, predictable vocabulary. Here is an illustrative call event:.

Consider a failure between these two operations: the application saves an event, then crashes before scheduling its CRM upgrade. The event exists, but nothing is waiting to deliver it.

A transactional outbox addresses that gap. Save the event and a delivery task in the same database transaction, then let a worker process the task. AWS explains this dual-write problem in its transactional outbox guidance.

According to recent reports, postgreSQL's INSERT documentation defines the conflict handling used here. The unique key makes duplicate detection hold across application processes. A duplicate with the same normalized payload creates no second task; reuse of the key with different data raises a conflict for investigation.

This depends on immutable event bodies. Do not add a fresh receipt timestamp, random identifier, or current CRM status to the normalized payload on each delivery. Store later enrichment separately or emit a newly introduced event. Otherwise an ordinary retry will appear to be a conflicting event.

The function deliberately uses one database client throughout the transaction, as required by the node-postgres transaction documentation. Parameter values are passed separately from SQL, following its parameterized query guidance.

Sources indicate that after this function commits, acknowledge the notification using the response expected by the sender. An identical duplicate should also receive a successful acknowledgement. If persistence fails, return the appropriate failure response and rely on the configured retry or reconciliation process. A success response sent before durable storage can turn a temporary database failure into a missing event.

In a recent development, for voice integrations, distinguish an informational status callback from a request asking your application how to handle a live call. They can require different response bodies, as explained in the Twilio webhooks FAQ.

The outbox gives you durable work to process. It does not make a remote CRM operation happen exactly once.

Imagine the CRM saves an upgrade, but the worker crashes before setting processed_at. When the task runs again, the same request may reach the CRM twice. Design for that case explicitly.

Sources indicate that use a stable external identifier for each contact, opportunity, and activity, and check which deduplication guarantees the destination supports. HubSpot's contacts API documentation, for example, describes upserts using unique properties. Support for a contact upsert does not automatically make every associated activity or workflow idempotent. Verify the behavior of each operation you send.

If the destination cannot deduplicate a create request and a timeout leaves its result uncertain, reconcile that operation before repeating it. A local “sent” flag alone cannot prove whether the remote write happened.

The worker should claim due tasks, commit a recoverable lease, and perform network calls outside the database transaction. A lease allows another worker to recover work after a crash. When multiple workers poll the outbox, PostgreSQL's SKIP LOCKED behavior can help claim separate rows, but the lease and its recovery logic still need to be implemented.

It has been revealed that retry transient failures with increasing delays and jitter. Respect the destination's rate-limit instructions. Send persistent validation failures to a review queue with a useful error category, and provide a way to replay them after correction. The schema above is the ingestion foundation; a production worker needs lease fields, failure details, and a retry policy appropriate to its destination.

It has been revealed that also preserve ordering where it changes meaning. If two events update the same contact or opportunity, process them serially or reject stale updates using a stored version. A historical event should not move a won opportunity back to an earlier stage.

Once both channels reach the CRM, connect them to the result the business cares about. A form submission is an inquiry. A completed phone call is a technical outcome. Neither alone establishes that a lead qualified or a purchase happened. If agents record call dispositions, such as whether a call was qualified or transferred to a closer, that field is a richer signal than call completion status alone.

In a recent development, have the CRM or the system that owns the transaction emit explicit outcome events, such as lead.qualified and deal.won. Include the internal opportunity ID and the original outcome time. Model reversals or cancellations explicitly if they affect revenue reporting.

Sources indicate that then choose the unit behind each metric. For a report about opportunities acquired during a particular month, a qualification rate can use qualified opportunities divided by all opportunities in that acquisition cohort. Counting qualification events received during the month would answer a different question and could include older inquiries.

In a recent development, deduplicate opportunities before calculating channel totals. A person who submits a form and calls about the same purchase should retain both interactions, while the opportunity receives credit according to your chosen attribution rule. Label that rule in the report so first-touch and last-touch numbers are not compared as though they measure the same thing.

In a recent development, measure data quality alongside performance. Track unresolved attribution, duplicate deliveries, ingestion failures, and the age of the oldest pending outbox task. Once several sources and destinations feed the same reports, a data observability platform can watch these signals across the whole pipeline instead of relying on checks inside a single worker. An apparently quiet campaign may actually have a broken integration.

Recent findings suggest that operational logs should contain enough context to investigate failures without becoming another customer database. Use internal references and error categories, and avoid dumping webhook bodies into logs. The OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet provides guidance on excluding or protecting sensitive values.

Sources indicate that A successful form submission proves little about retries or missing data. Before connecting production traffic, test the cases that could distort reporting or lose an inquiry.

Sources indicate that run database cases against PostgreSQL with separate connections so the tests exercise actual constraints and transaction behavior. Use the provider's test tools or signed fixtures for webhook authentication. Test CRM retries against a sandbox with the destination's real duplicate-handling rules.

Sources indicate that start rollout with one form and one phone source. Trace a known inquiry from its captured campaign through its interactions to its CRM outcome. Reconcile event totals against the source systems over the same time window, allowing for delivery delays. Expand once that path is explainable and failures are visible.

In a recent development, the same adapter pattern extends to inquiries that start offline, such as leads collected at a trade show and exported as a CSV or XLSX file. Import each row as a form.submitted event with the event as its source, a stable row identifier as event_id, and the original capture time as occurred_at. Because the outbox treats an identical event as a duplicate, re-importing the same export won’t create a second CRM task.

What is a unified lead tracking pipeline?

It is a workflow that converts inquiries from different channels into a shared data model, preserves their acquisition context, and connects them to business outcomes. Forms and calls keep their own interaction records, while contacts and opportunities provide the relationships needed for reporting.

Can I connect a phone call to a website visit?

Sometimes. Dynamic number insertion can provide a session or visitor association when the provider's mapping is available and valid. A campaign-specific number usually supports campaign-level attribution. If the caller uses a saved number, switches devices, or calls after a mapping expires, the available evidence may be less precise.

How do I prevent duplicate leads?

Handle duplicate delivery and identity resolution separately. Stable event IDs and a database constraint prevent repeated notifications from producing repeated work. Connecting several interactions to one contact or opportunity requires a separate matching policy, with ambiguous cases left unresolved until there is enough evidence.

Should a completed call count as a conversion?

Sources indicate that only if that is the conversion your report explicitly measures. A completed call does not establish that a prospect qualified or bought something. Keep technical call status separate from CRM outcomes and use the latter when reporting qualified demand or revenue.

Do I need a message broker for this architecture?

It has been revealed that you can begin with PostgreSQL and an outbox worker if that setup meets your throughput and latency needs. A broker becomes useful when several consumers need independent delivery, or when buffering and scale justify the additional operations. In either case, retries still require idempotent consumers.

What happens when tracking consent is unavailable?

Keep the inquiry flow usable and apply your site's existing consent rules to optional attribution collection and storage. Accept permitted form or call data, leave unavailable attribution empty, and avoid reconstructing a visitor identity through fingerprinting. Reports should expose that missing context instead of inventing a campaign match.
