📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With the flick of a switch, he smoked out competent PC maintenance skills.

Industry observers note that returning to work after the weekend can feel like voluntarily walking into a trap. To help readers feel a little freer, The Register therefore uses Monday mornings to serve up a fresh installment of "Who, Me?" It's the column in which we share your stories of mistakes, misjudgments, and occasional misanthropy.

This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Marshall," who told us about a job interview he endured about 20 years ago.

The interview included a practical component he described as "Here's a PC, we've broken a few things in it, get it going.".

Marshall swiftly spotted some mundane faults, such as a loose PCI card and unplugged internal cables.

Sources indicate that he felt the test was too easy. "One of the things I always checked was whether the power supply 110/230 switch was set for the UK," he told The Register.

Getting the PC running earned Marshall a job offer, but he couldn't resist suggesting a tougher test.

"I stated to my future manager: 'Would it be a good thing to set the power supply to the wrong voltage as part of the interview test?' He said that wasn't fair.".

In a recent development, marshall stayed in the job for two years. A couple of months after he left, his former manager sent him a short email.

Marshall asked another former colleague what might have prompted that email.

"It turned out somebody – I don't know if it was an interview candidate – had blown a power supply by not checking the voltage it was set to.".

What a coincidence! Or maybe not?

"It wasn't anything to do with me," Marshall insisted. "No idea who it was.".

According to recent reports, have you held colleagues to a higher standard than the boss expected? Or left a little trap for them to trip over? In either case, click here to send email to Who, Me? We appreciate the chance to share your stories, and do so with appropriate anonymization so that contributors never step into the jaws of trouble. ®.

De-fanging dangerous triggers in GitHub Actions across an organization

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (790 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Blogspot

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that on December 2, 2026, GitHub will start blocking the pull_request_target trigger by default in public repositories.
  • According to recent reports, the short version: a handful of GitHub Actions triggers let a stranger on the internet start a workflow that may have access to your secrets.
  • Mike Fiedler, PyPI Safety and Security Engineer, and Seth Larson, Security Developer in Residence, have removed dangerous triggers and applied these policies to the Python Software Foundation (PSF) stewarded GitHub organizations (psf, python, pypi).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that on December 2, 2026, GitHub will start blocking the pull_request_target trigger by default in public repositories. If that sentence means nothing to you, this post is for you. If it fills you with dread, it is also for you.

According to recent reports, the short version: a handful of GitHub Actions triggers let a stranger on the internet start a workflow that may have access to your secrets. On a GitHub Team or Enterprise proposal, you can turn them off for every repository in your organization with one policy. On a Free plan, you can do it one repository at a time. Set the policy up, check what it would block, then enforce it.

Mike Fiedler, PyPI Safety and Security Engineer, and Seth Larson, Security Developer in Residence, have removed dangerous triggers and applied these policies to the Python Software Foundation (PSF) stewarded GitHub organizations (psf, python, pypi). They also wrote up technical documentation on how to roll these policies out to your own projects and organizations. The full details and technical documentation are available on the Alpha-Omega blog.

Yes, repeatedly. A few that have affected projects hosted on PyPI directly:.

According to recent reports, ultralytics, December 2024. The project's GitHub Actions workflows were compromised and the build cache was poisoned, which put malicious releases on PyPI. Seth wrote PyPI's analysis. William Woodruff's write-up traces the entry point to a pull_request_target workflow.

It has been revealed that liteLLM and Telnyx, March 2026. Malicious releases of both packages were published after an API token was exposed through an exploited Trivy dependency. StepSecurity traced the Trivy compromise back to a pull_request_target workflow exploited three weeks earlier. We worked with both maintainer teams on token rotation, release removals, and moving to Trusted Publishers, which both projects have since adopted.

Recent findings suggest that elementary-data, April 2026. A workflow triggered by comments puts the comment text straight into a shell script. One crafted comment on a pull request ran with a token that could be written to the repository. The attacker used it to commit a malicious file and push a release tag, and the project's own release pipeline published the result to PyPI.

Sources indicate that the maintainers behind these projects weren't careless. These triggers look harmless in a workflow file, and the unsafe version is one line away from the safe one.

Insecure triggers can run workflows with access to your secrets, and a stranger can start them.

When someone opens a pull request from a fork, the pull_request trigger runs their code with a read-only token and no secrets. That's the safe one.

Industry observers note that pull_request_target looks almost the same in a workflow file and behaves very differently. It runs with a read/write token and access to your repository and organization secrets. GitHub built it for chores like labeling pull requests from forks, where the workflow never touches the contributor's code. The trouble starts when a workflow checks out the pull request and runs it anyway:.

Anyone with a GitHub account can open that pull request. Their code now runs with your credentials. This is called a "pwn request", and GitHub's docs describe it as the root cause of multiple supply-chain compromises.

In a recent development, the issue_comment trigger carries the same risk. This trigger fires when anyone comments on an issue or pull request, and the workflow runs with the repository's token and secrets. Sometimes the victim is a "comment /test to run CI" bot that checks out the pull request and runs their code. Sometimes the workflow pastes the comment text into a templated shell command, and the comment turns out to inject different instructions into the workflow shell.

That support is what gives us the time for the work behind this post:.

Seth wrote PyPI's analysis of the Ultralytics attack.

Mike and Seth worked with the LiteLLM and Telnyx maintainers during their incident, and wrote up the guidance for everyone else.

Mike set up the event policy for the pypi GitHub organization.

Seth is working to migrate the few remaining repositories using insecure triggers in the python GitHub organization before enabling the event policy.

Mike and Seth wrote this guide so other organizations can do the same!

Recent findings suggest that the PSF is a non-profit whose mission is to promote, protect, and advance the Python programming language, and to support and facilitate the growth of a diverse and international community of Python programmers. The PSF supports the Python community using corporate sponsorships, grants, and donations. Are you interested in sponsoring or donating to the PSF so it can continue supporting Python and its community? Check out our sponsorship program, donate directly here, or contact our team!

Granite 4.1 LLMs: How They’re Built

📅 29 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1726 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An in-depth technical walkthrough of data engineering, pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning behind the Granite 4.1 LLMs.
  • It has been revealed that TL;DR — Granite 4.1 is a family of dense, decoder‑only LLMs (3B, 8B, and 30B) trained on ~15T tokens using a multi‑stage pre‑training pipeline, including long‑context extension of up to 512K tokens.
  • Building high‑quality small language models goes beyond simply scaling compute—it requires rigorous data curation throughout training.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An in-depth technical walkthrough of data engineering, pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning behind the Granite 4.1 LLMs.

It has been revealed that TL;DR — Granite 4.1 is a family of dense, decoder‑only LLMs (3B, 8B, and 30B) trained on ~15T tokens using a multi‑stage pre‑training pipeline, including long‑context extension of up to 512K tokens. The models are further refined with supervised fine‑tuning on ~4.1M high‑quality curated samples and reinforcement learning via on‑policy GRPO with DAPO loss (Yu et al., 2025). Notably, the 8B instruct model matches or surpasses the previous Granite 4.0‑H‑Small (32B‑A9B MoE) despite using a simpler dense architecture with fewer parameters. All Granite 4.1 models are released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Building high‑quality small language models goes beyond simply scaling compute—it requires rigorous data curation throughout training. For Granite 4.1, we prioritized data quality over quantity, progressively refining the data mixture across five pre‑training stages. We further curated supervised fine‑tuning data using an LLM‑as‑Judge framework and applied a multi‑stage reinforcement learning pipeline to systematically strengthen performance in math, coding, instruction following, and general chat.

Granite 4.1 models use a decoder-only dense transformer architecture. The core design choices include Grouped Query Attention (GQA), Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE), SwiGLU activations, RMSNorm, and shared input/output embeddings.

All three model sizes share the same training pipeline and data strategy, differing only in architecture dimensions.

Granite 4.1 is trained from scratch on approximately 15 trillion tokens using a five‑phase training strategy. Phases 1–2 focus on foundational pre‑training, phases 3–4 perform mid‑training with progressively higher‑quality data annealing, and phase 5 introduces long‑context training, extending the context window to 512K tokens. Each phase employs a distinct data mixture and learning‑rate schedule, gradually shifting from broad web‑scale data to more curated, domain‑specific content.

Figure 2: The five-phase pre-training pipeline. Phases 1–2 are pre-training, Phases 3–4 are mid-training (high-quality data annealing), and Phase 5 is long context training (LCE).

The first phase establishes broad language understanding using a general mixture of training data with a power learning rate schedule and warmup.

Phase 2 sharply increases the proportion of code and mathematical data, pivoting toward stronger reasoning capabilities while still maintaining general language coverage.

Recent findings suggest that phase 3 transitions into mid-training with a more balanced, high-quality mixture and an exponential decay learning rate schedule. This is where we start blending in chain-of-thought and synthetic instruction data.

The fourth phase continues mid-training with a linear learning rate decay to zero, focusing the model on the highest-quality data available.

Figure 3: How the data mix evolves across the pre-training phases. Notice the progressive shift from web-heavy (Phase 1) to quality-heavy with instruction and reasoning data (Phases 3–4).

The fifth and final phase also part of of mid-training extends the context window from 4K to 512K through a staged long-context extension process:.

In a recent development, the LCE phase uses an exponential learning rate schedule starting at 1e-4 and decaying to 0. To ensure the model natively handles long sequences without degrading short-context performance, we do a model merge after each LCE stage. RULER benchmark of base models:.

Industry observers note that supervised fine‑tuning (SFT) is what turns the base model into a reliable instruction‑following assistant, making data quality critically key—since even a small number of incorrect or hallucinated samples can instill undesirable behaviors. To address this, we apply a rigorous LLM‑as‑Judge framework alongside rule‑based filtering to curate high-quality samples. Together, the pipeline automatically assess each sample against structural, semantic, and behavioral criteria, fixing issues when possible and filtering out samples that fail to meet our quality standards.

Sources indicate that figure 4: The SFT data quality pipeline. Raw conversation data passes through an LLM-as-Judge with a multi-dimensional rubric, producing accept/borderline/reject verdicts. Hard-reject defects (hallucination, false premise, incorrect computation) trigger automatic rejection regardless of score.

In a recent development, our rigorous LLM‑as‑Judge framework evaluates only assistant responses, treating system prompts, user inputs, retrieved documents, and tool outputs strictly as contextual information. This ensures that the judge assesses what the model notes, rather than what it was asked to do. In RAG settings, responses that are not grounded in the retrieved context are flagged as hallucinations, while tool‑use outputs are validated against the set of allowed tools and their parameter schemas.

It has been revealed that we employ specialized judge prompts tailored to different SFT data types, including multi‑turn dialogue, RAG‑augmented responses, tool‑calling interactions, and multilingual conversations. Each response is scored across six weighted dimensions—instruction following, correctness, completeness, conciseness, naturalness, and calibration (with optional critical‑thinking checks). Samples are accepted, flagged as borderline, or rejected based on deterministic score thresholds, with hard‑reject rules overriding scores for severe defects such as hallucinations, false premises, or incorrect computations.

According to recent reports, to complement semantic evaluation, we apply a deterministic rule‑based pipeline that enforces structural integrity through text normalization, truncation and length filtering, schema validation, and leakage detection. A final global deduplication step ensures dataset‑wide uniqueness. All filtering and correction actions are fully auditable.

After passing through the LLM-as-Judge, rule-based filtering, and global deduplication pipeline, we fine-tune base models on these approximately 4.1 million high-quality samples. The following details apply to all three model variants:.

Sources indicate that after SFT, we apply a multi-stage reinforcement learning pipeline to further improve the model's capabilities across specific domains. Rather than a single RL pass, we run multiple targeted RL stages, each optimizing for different capabilities.

We use On-policy GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) (Shao et al., 2024) with DAPO (Decoupled Clip and Dynamic sAmpling Policy Optimization) loss (Yu et al., 2025) which provides more stable training signals compared to standard GRPO. However, due to computationally intensive nature of dynamic sampling, we switch it off during our training runs.

According to recent reports, figure 10 depicts our Reinforcement Learning pipeline for training Granite 4.1 models. Through extensive experimentation with a variety of reinforcement learning recipes, we found that this sequence of steps minimizes catastrophic forgetting while simultaneously maximizing performance across multiple domains.

Figure 10: The Granite 4.1 reinforcement learning pipeline consisting of four sequential stages: Multi-domain RL, RLHF, Identity and Knowledge-calibration RL, and Math RL.

According to recent reports, in this stage, the model is trained jointly on a unified mixture of data drawn from multiple domains. Every gradient update therefore reflects the full diversity of tasks, which prevents catastrophic forgetting, boosts overall benchmark performance, and minimizes regressions on any individual task.

The different domains covered in this stage include:.

During this stage, we trained the models on 45,504 unique prompts (averaged across all Granite 4.1 models) and found that a learning rate of 5e‑7 with a KL‑loss coefficient ($\beta$) of 0.05 performed best for multi‑domain reinforcement learning.

Recent findings suggest that to further improve the model's helpfulness and chat ability, we train our model on generic-chat prompts using a multilingual scalar reward model. With this stage, we observed an average improvement of ~18.9 points (averaged across the three Granite 4.1 models) in Alpaca-Eval compared to the SFT checkpoints.

It has been revealed that to mitigate policy drift from its previously learned knowledge, we use a conservative learning rate of 3e-7 and higher KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.09 in this stage. We use an average of 17,920 unique prompts in this RLHF stage.

It has been revealed that in this stage, we train the model for a few steps (~40 training steps) on identity and knowledge calibration prompts. We observed that this small training stage significantly improves the model's self-identification capabilities.

Similar to the RLHF stage, we used a learning rate of 3e-7 and KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.09, and we use 1728 unique prompts in this stage.

Sources indicate that during our RL training, we found that the RLHF stage causes a drop in math benchmark scores (e.g., in GSM8K, DeepMind-Math). The Math RL stage enables the model to recover from this drop and surpasses the original SFT performance on math benchmarks: ~3.8 points on average for GSM8K, and ~23.48 points on average for DeepMind-Math. We use an average of 13,504 unique prompts in this stage and similar to the multi-domain RL stage, we used a learning rate of 5e-7 and KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.05.

Supported languages: English, German, Spanish, French, Japanese, Portuguese, Arabic, Czech, Italian, Korean, Dutch, and Chinese.

In a recent development, granite 4.1 delivers competitive instruction‑following and tool‑calling capabilities without relying on long chains of thought. By avoiding extended reasoning traces, it provides predictable latency, stable token usage, and lower operational cost. This makes Granite 4.1 a production‑ready, open‑source choice for enterprise workloads where efficiency, reliability, and cost control are critical.

A striking result: the Granite 4.1-8B dense model consistently matches or outperforms the previous-generation Granite 4.0-H-Small, a 32B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 9B active parameters.

Figure 13: Granite 4.1-8B (dark blue) vs. Granite 4.0-H-Small 32B-A9B (light blue) across benchmarks. The 8B dense model matches or exceeds the larger MoE model on IFEval, AlpacaEval, MMLU-Pro, BBH, GSM8K, DeepMind-Math, Evalplus, ArenaHard, BFCL V3 and MBPP(+).

Industry observers note that figure 14: Comparison across the Granite 4.1 family — 30B, 8B, and 3B models. Scores scale predictably with model size, with the 30B model leading across all benchmarks.

Industry observers note that we also released fp8 quantized variants of the Granite 4.1 models, optimized for inference with vLLM. The precision is reduced from 16‑bit to 8‑bit, resulting in approximately a 50% reduction in both disk footprint and GPU memory usage. Quantization is applied only to the weights and activations of linear operators within the transformer blocks using LLM Compressor, while all other layers are preserved at their original precision.

We trained the Granite 4.1 Language Models on an NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 cluster hosted on CoreWeave:.

This infrastructure provides the scalable, high-bandwidth interconnect needed for efficient distributed training at the token volumes required (15T+ tokens across pre-training alone).

Granite 4.1 models are available under the Apache 2.0 license. Here's how to get started with the 30B instruct model wiht tool calling example:.

Granite 4.1 marks a significant step forward for high‑quality, open‑source language models. By prioritizing data quality and rigor at every stage—from pre‑training curation to supervised fine‑tuning and multi‑stage reinforcement learning—we deliver a substantially improved post‑training pipeline. The result is stronger instruction following, tool use, and conversational performance, showing that carefully trained dense 8B models can rival much larger MoE architectures. We’re excited to see how the community adopts and builds on these models.

Lean and Mathlib Communities Certify Claude-Assisted Riemann Proof

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (886 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Lean and Mathlib communities certified on November 21, 2026 that Levent Alpöge’s 17-million-line Lean library correctly states and proves the Riemann Hypothesis, following a day of compilation, statement-matching, and proof-kernel checks.
  • The certification follows Alpöge’s announcement on November 20, 2026, in which he said he discovered and formalized the proof while working with Claude.
  • Sources indicate that the codebase depends directly only on Mathlib, the community’s library of formalized mathematics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Lean and Mathlib communities certified on November 21, 2026 that Levent Alpöge’s 17-million-line Lean library correctly states and proves the Riemann Hypothesis, following a day of compilation, statement-matching, and proof-kernel checks. Their joint statement was endorsed by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative.

The certification follows Alpöge’s announcement on November 20, 2026, in which he said he discovered and formalized the proof while working with Claude. The release contained only the Lean formalization; Alpöge viewed a conventional write-up at this stage as a huge, unreadable document and planned to understand, simplify, and explain the mathematics properly.

Sources indicate that the codebase depends directly only on Mathlib, the community’s library of formalized mathematics. The statement being proved was already part of Mathlib and had been vetted by experts in Lean and number theory, addressing the requirement that the formal statement express the intended hypothesis. Dozens of people reported compiling the library without errors or build failures and reproducing the same raw proof export.

To check the theorem’s identity, a community-added challenge file isolated the Riemann Hypothesis statement and imported only Mathlib. Comparator and con-leche’s comparison mode independently confirmed that Alpöge’s theorem matched that statement exactly. The raw proof export was checked with Lean’s official kernel, con-leche, con-ron, and additional third-party checkers written in different programming languages.

Sources indicate that those checks ran on an inert export, beyond the reach of hypothetical malicious code in the Lean sources. Con-leche and con-ron also have formal proofs, relative to set theory, that they cannot accept a false proof, addressing concerns that a flaw in Lean’s logic could be exploited.

Sources indicate that andrew Sutherland’s MIT verification record, last updated at 12:55 UTC on November 21, 2026, reports that all 175,187 modules compiled with zero errors using Lean and Mathlib version 4.33.1; his checks were run with Claude Code. An axiom audit found that the five headline theorems depended only on propext, Classical.choice, and Quot.sound, with no axioms declared outside Lean core. Nanoda, an independent Rust kernel, and con-leche each accepted the full exported proof, lean4lean accepted every compiled module, and con-leche’s comparison mode matched every challenge statement.

At that page’s cutoff, the Lean default and paranoid kernel checks on the export and the full lake comparator run remained in progress. Older bundled con-leche and con-ron binaries exited without a verdict because they did not support one reflexive inductive type, not because they rejected the proof. Sutherland also disclosed that the build ran on unsandboxed cloud machines and that its export hash had not been compared with one from a sandboxed lake build; a passing result still relies on the kernels used and on Mathlib’s definitions representing their intended mathematics.

Recent findings suggest that the central theorem uses Mathlib’s formal definition: every zero of the Riemann zeta function other than the trivial zeros at negative even integers must have real part one-half. The separate condition s ≠ 1 appears because Mathlib assigns the zeta function a conventional value at its pole. The submission also verifies Generalized Riemann Hypothesis statements for Dirichlet L-functions across all moduli and characters; Sutherland expressly excludes Dedekind zeta functions, Hecke L-functions, and general automorphic L-functions from the checked scope.

Alpöge’s account assigns Claude a role in discovery as well as formalization: he guided the work from a toy setting into an analogous target situation before Claude outpaced him near the finish. In one example, Claude suggested that a von Mangoldt sum of length X should use a chain of theta lifts of length X, a technical choice Alpöge highlights in his explanation of the argument.

Alpöge describes the current argument as extremely long, expects substantial simplification, and is still working to understand and explain it. His account describes human guidance and Claude’s technical contributions, with both formalizing the arguments without extra assumptions. The certification concerns the formal artifact; that account supplies the basis for describing Claude’s role, rather than demonstrating an autonomous solution.

Industry observers note that the certification resolves the formal-checking question without resolving the explanatory one. Whether the proof’s new ideas can be simplified and absorbed by mathematicians remains the central open question around the verified Lean library.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Terraform proposal passes and indicates all green and all the necessary resource changes.
  • The problem with the difference between blueprint and apply jobs is that plan can't possibly emulate every actual API call against a live infrastructure.
  • Sources indicate that there are multiple tools that can emulate AWS services either partially or in full, but what they lack is the actual knowledge of the service architecture.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Terraform proposal passes and indicates all green and all the necessary resource changes. You trigger apply and... the job fails with some obscure error that a resource can't be changed. You open another pull request and try again. And perhaps you encounter an error again. Sounds familiar? I bet it does. I encountered issues like this so many times I'm afraid to count. But recently AWS released a latest tool called Emulator that emulates actual AWS API endpoints. And it should be great for tasks just like that!

The problem with the difference between blueprint and apply jobs is that plan can't possibly emulate every actual API call against a live infrastructure. It's a safe assumption based on the static declarations we put into it – the order of application, the necessary parameters, the proper configuration values. These mock calls can't know for a fact that you already have a resource in AWS called "my-bucket-asdasdasd" or that you're trying to upgrade a PostgreSQL RDS instance from version 14 to version 18 without an explicit "apply immediately" flag. One may argue that one can always try to apply changes locally, but this kinda undermines the whole automation workflow. So what is the answer?

Sources indicate that there are multiple tools that can emulate AWS services either partially or in full, but what they lack is the actual knowledge of the service architecture. It may be similar, but it won't be authentic, and sometimes this small difference may cause a lot of problems. After all, what can be the closest to an AWS API, if not the same AWS API, but ephemeral?

Sources indicate that the benefit of the AWS Emulator is that it's a self-contained binary (or Docker container) that can be utilized locally or in a CI workflow. This means the usual "Strategy > Apply" terraform workflow changes to "Plan > Apply against mock AWS infrastructure to test the plan > Apply on actual AWS Infrastructure". This means slightly longer jobs, but if you're like me and apply jobs run on commits to the main branch after a PR, this saves you the hassle of creating a new branch just to fix the issue.

Sources indicate that let's start with a local setup and see how we can utilize AWS Emulator with the actual Terraform code. All code is available in my example GitHub repository.

Industry observers note that first up, installation. You can either install aws-emulator via package manager, or build it with Docker. I'll use Docker to keep my system clear of yet another package:.

Sources indicate that and it's up and running! In the example above I set the container to live without limits (official AWS documentation proposes to set memory and swap limits: --memory=2g --memory-swap=2g, but for local that's fine). I also disabled authorization (flag -a off) to simplify things a bit.

To be sure aws-emulator is up and running, let's query the admin endpoint:.

Okay, fake AWS is live, let's deploy some infrastructure!

I created an example AWS stack for Terraform and will use it in this article. First, let's configure Terraform to act against aws-emulator and not real AWS APIs. providers.tf will look like this:.

The difference between actual live infrastructure and a fake one is that we set up a bunch of flags to allow insecure connections (perhaps turning authentication off wasn't actually simpler?) and we set up an endpoint for each service we use in the setup to an emulator endpoint, which lives in the local Docker container:.

Industry observers note that the rest of the configuration is as usual: resources, variables, modules (if any). Just what your project has.

Let's proceed and test our setup. (I'll omit full terraform output otherwise this article would be 3 kilometers long).

In a recent development, strategy works! That's good to see, but not what we're here for. Still, a good sign. Now for the real test.

Sadly, the running aws-emulator container doesn't show in its logs which API requests it receives and what's happening under the hood, but I guess the tool is good enough as it is.

When you're done, stop the container:.

A container started with --rm removes itself after stopping, so no additional cleanup is needed. And as for the emulator -- it stores its state in memory, so each container restart drops all record of previous actions and any stale state.

Now for the real test: can we wrap the desired logic inside a CI pipeline? Let's think.

For successful invocation in the pipeline we will need almost everything the same, but we will be limited by time (the faster -- the better, and overall reasonable timeouts) and resources.

Recent findings suggest that the workflow with terraform apply against aws-emulator is shown down below. For it I decided to try out package manager installation (builders are ephemeral anyway) and proper authentication. Full workflow with actual successful runs can be found in the example GitHub repository.

This is a crude excerpt of the actual glorious workflow file that outlines the most crucial steps: emulator installation, terraform setup, plan and apply. On the example terraform architecture the whole pipeline took 1m25s, which is okay in my opinion, but there is room for improvement: sprinkle some caching on top, leave validation, format check for local hooks, etc.

In a recent development, it's always nice when code someone wrote on the internet works from the start after you copy-paste it onto your machine. That's why I always run the described processes myself -- building, testing, fixing, retrying -- before publishing an article. But showing only the positive scenarios creates a false sense of trust in the tool.

Let's break something on purpose.

Industry observers note that in the example codebase I added a variable that, when enabled, makes the stack try to deploy a resource with an erroneous declaration. It will pass the plan job, but fail on apply.

In a recent development, setting this variable to true at runtime will break our stack. Let's see:.

Sources indicate that and there we have it. The exact concern that arises only against actual API calls and not during a plan job.

For scenarios exactly like this, the emulator is priceless.

It has been revealed that AWS Emulator is AWESOME. I'm rarely that excited about fresh tools lately (mostly because almost all of them are near/about AI), but this one is just so good and scratches that exact itch I felt for so long.

In a recent development, for starters, it can't effectively emulate IAM policies and permission checks. This is a bummer, because permission validation is such a crucial step for production-ready security. Here's hoping that the tool will evolve further and it will be included in future updates.

Recent findings suggest that second, as a tool still a work-in-progress[1], its capabilities are quite limited. Even while writing the article I encountered several cases of 501 NotImplemented. It complicates things a bit if your infrastructure setup is huge and has a lot of quirks and weird configurations and super fresh services. Still, AWS releases new versions quite often, and they're quite open about Emulator limitations, which is nice.

And last, but not least, is telemetry. AWS is explicit that it gathers telemetry and what this telemetry includes. This is honest behaviour and I like that approach. They even allow you to disable the telemetry, which further increases my trust in this tool. I understand the rationale behind this functionality (the tool is actively developed, they need the data to understand usage patterns and what goes wrong), but in the age of constant surveillance from Big Tech at every corner it still raises a slight concern. But then again, for the ultra-paranoid folks the code is open source and can be rebuilt with telemetry torn out of it.

As of the moment of writing this article, AWS Emulator has been live for 1 day. ↩︎.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." (Goodhart’s Law).
  • It has been revealed that TLDR: Appen Inc.
  • We’re not updating the average WER at this time: by default, the leaderboard’s Average WER remains computed on public datasets only.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." (Goodhart’s Law).

It has been revealed that TLDR: Appen Inc. and DataoceanAI have provided high-quality English ASR datasets covering scripted and conversational speech over multiple accents. To prevent potential risks of benchmaxxing or test-set contamination, we will keep these datasets private for a high-quality measure of performance on multiple tasks.

We’re not updating the average WER at this time: by default, the leaderboard’s Average WER remains computed on public datasets only. You can optionally include the private datasets using the toggle to see their impact 👀.

Since its launch in September 2023, the Open ASR Leaderboard has been visited over 710K times. We’re blown away by the community’s interest and motivation to keep pushing speech recognition 🗣️.

Two words sum up the objectives (but also challenges) in maintaining a benchmark like the Open ASR Leaderboard:.

Standardization: models can have different conventions for their usage and outputs, e.g. with/without punctuation and casing. Datasets have the same challenges and can be structured differently. To this end, all test sets have been gathered into a single dataset on the Hub for easy access and previewing. Moreover, to standardize model outputs and dataset transcripts, we use a normalizer that (among other things) removes punctuation and casing, and maps to American spelling. It is based on the normalizer of Whisper.

Openness: the UI code and evaluation scripts are open-sourced. This has helped not only to incorporate new models, but also to improve the quality of the evaluation procedure through community feedback and contributions.

Standardization and openness are essential for meaningful benchmarking, but they also make benchmarks more susceptible to benchmark-specific optimization ("benchmaxxing"), where models improve leaderboard performance without corresponding gains in real-world robustness. As models and use cases evolve, the Open ASR Leaderboard will continue incorporating high-quality datasets and newly introduced evaluation settings to better reflect real-world performance and improve robustness against benchmark-specific optimization.

According to recent reports, as discussed in our report, there is no single "catch-all" ASR model: some perform better on American English, others on diverse accents and multilingual settings, while others are optimized for speed or conversational audio. Different applications also prioritize different capabilities, so a model that performs less well on one dimension is not necessarily a worse model overall. The goal of the Open ASR Leaderboard is to capture these nuances and provide a more holistic view of ASR performance.

Recent findings suggest that to this end, we have worked with Appen Inc. and DataoceanAI to curate high-quality datasets for ASR benchmarking. Below is some information on the various splits.

Below are sample audio showing the variety of content (scripted, conversational, acronyms, disfluencies, proper nouns).

While private datasets may sound contrary to the spirit of openness, we believe that incorporating such datasets will increase the trustworthiness of the Open ASR Leaderboard, as they are less likely to be exploited for benchmaxxing, whether by model developers who explicitly use the public test sets or who try to find training data that closely resembles a particular dataset to boost their score in the macroaverage.

According to recent reports, with these datasets, we can also provide targeted metrics to highlight gaps and biases between controlled and often saturated settings (scripted, American accent) and more nuanced conditions (conversational and non-American accents). Below is a screenshot of the newly introduced "Private data" tab.

Below is how each column is computed.

We intentionally do not provide a score on each split, to avoid model developers from boosting their score with a specific data provider or accent.

It has been revealed that get your model on the Open ASR Leaderboard, and we'll run the evaluation! As before, the process for adding a model to the leaderboard takes place on the Open ASR Leaderboard GitHub:.

While you wait for your model to be added to the Open ASR Leaderboard, you can self-report your metrics on the public sets by adding a YAML file like this to your model card. Your model will then appear on an (unverified) leaderboard that appears on the dataset page (see screenshot below). More on this approach to decentralized evaluation can be read here.

They could. We’ve asked Appen and DataoceanAI to not provide this data to their clients. But even if they do not provide this exact data, data from a similar distribution could still help the model on the corresponding evaluation set (similar to benchmaxxing by optimizing for a challenging task from the public sets). To this end, having multiple data providers balances out the advantage a model may get from having used data from one of the providers. And we are open to more data providers and eval sets for the "Private data" tab!

Moreover, to ensure that the private sets do not affect the model ranking, we’ve defaulted the Average WER to not include the Private sets in its macroaverage.

In the screenshot below, you can see that "Private data" is toggled off. This means that the macroaverage across datasets does not include it.

Simply toggle on "Private data" splits to include them in the macroaverage.

Industry observers note that the "Rank Δ" column highlights how the ordering changes relative to the default macroaverage configuration. Including or excluding public datasets also changes the macroaverage, allowing owners to tailor the evaluation to the use cases and data distributions most relevant to their application.

We’re excited to hear the community’s feedback on how the fresh track and dataset toggling features help people identify the model(s) that best fit their application(s). We’re also looking into evaluations that better reflect real-world noisy conditions, and you can expect some news on that 😉.

Industry observers note that while preparing the private evaluation sets, we took extra care to ensure consistent audio and transcript quality across datasets, including developing tooling to identify challenging cases such as low signal-to-noise conditions or transcript mismatches, since these factors can meaningfully affect WER. More on that in a future post!

Just a quick observation on how we evaluate our models: The two data vendors mentioned earlier are offering datasets directly to ASR service providers for training. With that in mind, it feels like we should be extra prudent about mixing private data into our evaluations.

At the same time, we're missing out on a lot of high-quality, open-source speech datasets simply because their creators don't have sales teams advocating for them. It would be a huge step forward to open a channel where the research community can recommend these datasets to the leaderboard directly.

P.S. I found myself relating a lot to King George in the movie Hoppers recently. That beaver king just believes the best about everyone. I want to bring that same optimism here—hoping that everyone continues to follow the leaderboard rules, avoids training on open-source test sets, and actively cleans their training data of any contamination.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that together AI disclosed on November 21, 2026 that an unauthorized party downloaded stored samples from a subset of customer prompts submitted to its serverless inference service.
  • Industry observers note that customers had authorized the prompts for routine software testing, and Together AI stored the samples in a private Hugging Face repository.
  • Sources indicate that the coding agent committed a credential that granted access to the private Hugging Face repository during xorl’s development.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that together AI disclosed on November 21, 2026 that an unauthorized party downloaded stored samples from a subset of customer prompts submitted to its serverless inference service. An AI coding agent had exposed the private-repository credential used in the download while the company was developing its public xorl GitHub repository.

Industry observers note that customers had authorized the prompts for routine software testing, and Together AI stored the samples in a private Hugging Face repository. They involved requests to the MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2 and Kimi K2.6 models, primarily on June 24, 2026, July 4, 2026, July 8, 2026 and July 14, 2026.

Sources indicate that the coding agent committed a credential that granted access to the private Hugging Face repository during xorl’s development. Together AI’s automated scanning detected the exposure, and the company reverted the commit. During that exposure window, an unauthorized party obtained the credential and used it to download the stored samples.

The sequence makes clear that detecting and reverting the commit did not prevent the credential from being used during the exposure window. The model names establish which requests were sampled, while the repository credential explains how the stored prompts became accessible.

After the download, the party searched the samples for credentials to other services and tested whether they were valid. Five of the tested credentials were canary credentials associated with a Dragos security experiment. The searches and validity tests show that the activity extended to possible reuse of secrets contained in prompts, creating a risk beyond disclosure of the prompt text itself.

Together AI worked with an external forensic investigation firm and law enforcement. The organization said its review has not identified evidence of additional prompt leakage beyond this incident, that it has no reason to believe the data was leaked further, and that it understands the data has now been deleted.

Customer impact still depends on the content of the samples. The review is ongoing to determine whether sensitive personal information or other customer data was exposed, and Together AI will contact affected customers directly as needed with findings relevant to them.

It has been revealed that together AI’s response includes scoped or short-lived credentials and keyless access where supported, credential checks on all pull requests, and updated development processes governing the use of AI coding agents. The organization said the credential measures are designed to reduce the potential impact of exposure, while the other changes add controls around pull requests and coding-agent development.

Sources indicate that zero data retention, abbreviated ZDR, is now the default setting for newly introduced accounts. Together AI recommends that customers handling sensitive prompt data enable ZDR in their account settings and provides security@together.ai for questions about the incident or its potential impact on an organization.

The incident connects credential safety in AI-assisted development with the retention of customer prompts for testing. Together AI has documented controls for both, but the ongoing content review remains the decisive step in establishing what the exposure means for customers and which notifications are necessary.

NixOS bring-up on an Alibaba RISC-V board

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2098 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Feyor

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the process of scouring Alibaba for a cheap Versal devkit, I unexpectedly came into possession of a Zhihe Computing A210 RISC-V SoC.1.
  • It has been revealed that it’s a cool board: there’s a ridiculous amount of IO exposed by the baseboard, not to mention 8 cores clocked at 1.9 GHz is nothing to sniff at for a RISC-V CPU.
  • I decided to make this board into a NixOS build server so I could learn more about the state of RISC-V support in NixOS and to get some practice in Linux bringup.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the process of scouring Alibaba for a cheap Versal devkit, I unexpectedly came into possession of a Zhihe Computing A210 RISC-V SoC.1.

It has been revealed that it’s a cool board: there’s a ridiculous amount of IO exposed by the baseboard, not to mention 8 cores clocked at 1.9 GHz is nothing to sniff at for a RISC-V CPU. I’m not sure I could recommend buying any RISC-V SoC currently2, but all these distros that are starting to support RISC-V need to run tests somewhere that isn’t Spike/QEMU.

I decided to make this board into a NixOS build server so I could learn more about the state of RISC-V support in NixOS and to get some practice in Linux bringup.

My complete A210 NixOS configuration can be found here; I confirmed sound, HDMI, Bluetooth/Wi-Fi, ethernet, and the GPU were all working, but YMMV.

Nix makes cross compiling to RISC-V a breeze:.

It really is that easy—building pkgs.hello will produce a bona fide RISC-V executable (you don’t even need a Nix file for one-off builds, just run nix build nixpkgs#pkgsCross.riscv64.hello). Some black magic in callPackage ensures that compile-time tools are built for buildPlatform and build artifacts are built for hostPlatform.

In the process of compiling over a thousand packages I only ran into two challenges: a problem with rust-bindgen using the wrong version of clang and ministream not being properly configured for cross compilation, neither of which was specific to RISC-V.

Recent findings suggest that that having been mentioned, I did run into some pretty bizarre OOM issues for some of the heavy hitters like Clang and GFortran. I was seeing >9GB memory usage per linking process(!) when compiling from x86_64-linux, which will quickly exhaust all of your memory if you have max-jobs/cores set to sane values. I sidestepped this issue by temporarily nerfing build parallelism into oblivion and running the offending builds overnight:.

I don’t (yet) have access to a RISC-V remote Nix builder, but even if I did, it’s substantially faster to cross compile everything from my desktop. Cross compilation can get a little wonky with Nix flakes because you have to encode the buildPlatform in the output schema somehow, but nixosConfigurations does not allow nesting (nixosConfigurations.x86_64-linux-a210 is valid, but nixosConfigurations.x86_64-linux.a210 isn’t).

My solution to this is to expose the relevant build artifacts of the NixOS configuration (ISO + flashing script) under packages.${system} by creating a “wrapper” NixOS configuration for each buildPlatform that extends nixosConfigurations.a210:.

This way nixosConfigurations is agnostic to buildPlatform, and cross compilation is straightforward—running nix build .#image on an x86_64-linux machine will use x86_64-linux as the buildPlatform, as one would expect.

Ok, so the goal is to boot U-Boot FSBL -> OpenSBI -> U-Boot SSBL -> Linux -> NixOS userspace, using the vendor’s Buildroot scripts as reference.

Using vendor forks of U-Boot/Linux/OpenSBI is a simple matter of overriding src and sprinkling in a few patches (almost always to fix compiler warnings that have been promoted to errors in the latest version of GCC/Clang in nixpkgs). All we really have to do is slot in the vendor kernel by setting boot.kernelPackages = pkgs.linuxPackagesFor pkgs.linuxA210;.

Armed with a bootloader and NixOS image, I plugged in the A210 to my MacBook and turned on Fastboot flashing mode, but to my dismay macOS refused to enumerate the device. Initially I figured the board was a lemon (due to it being a freebie and all), but I wasn’t ready to give up hope that easily.

Recent findings suggest that I pored over the datasheet looking for alternative boot methods, and I investigated using PD resistors to force QSPI boot (using NORbert in lieu of a real QSPI device) to bootstrap into Linux userspace, at which point I could flash the eMMC directly without relying on Fastboot. But before pulling out my soldering iron I decided to try plugging the board into a different computer, which instantly detected the board. D’oh!

Ok, so Fastboot works3 and I’m able to load the flasher firmware and program eMMC (I based my Fastboot payload on openEuler’s A210 guide instead of the vendor’s script which flashes 7(!) different partitions), but after that I still got dead silence on UART. At this point I was pretty suspicious of my serial connection, so I decided to test it on a Pi Pico: lo and behold, it turns out leaving my BMP’s vRef pin floating was the culprit.

After losing several hours and my dignity to the aforementioned skill glitch, I was greeted with the following panic:.

Judging from the above register dump, something seems to be amiss with OpenSBI itself:.

In a recent development, this confirmed my suspicion that the illegal instruction was from an ISA extension (in this case, a vector instruction). Initially I didn’t understand why this occurred: why would a CPU trap on an instruction it supports? I consulted the ISA spec and discovered that executing a vector instruction without the vector context bits of the mstatus register configured properly will result in the exact illegal instruction exception that I was seeing.

In a recent development, so roughly what was happening was the processor was context switching to OpenSBI where the vector context was not enabled, but certain operations like memset were optimized to use vector extensions because OpenSBI was compiled with -march=rv64gv. I conjecture that the vendor didn’t run into this problem because they compiled OpenSBI with a GCC toolchain that didn’t support vector instructions, but who’s to say? Backporting a patch that sets -march=generic did the trick, and now we’re making it into U-Boot stage 2.

In a recent development, at this point I could boot Linux from eMMC manually, but I wanted to take the time to do things “right”. I prefer the more generic distro boot to the hard coded boot command the vendor came up with, so I decided to roll my own board header.

In a recent development, ok—now we’re able to get most of the way through the initrd before UART abruptly goes silent. Fortunately, the last message makes the problem pretty clear:.

Sources indicate that it’s a bit of a hack, but I decided to set clk_ignore_unused on the kernel command line just to see if we could get more logs. Imagine my surprise when after reflashing, the board makes it all the way into NixOS userspace with no issues! Although I steeled my resolve to go spelunking in the device tree to find which clock was not marked as critical, I decided not to waste my time when I realized the vendor also sets clk_ignore_unused in their kernel cmdline. ¯\_(ツ)_/¯.

I would be remiss if I didn’t mention that running an old kernel in the current era of AI-assisted kernel vulnerability disclosures hitting LKML every other week does not exactly help me sleep better at night. I looked into backporting patches for Dirty Frag and co., but if the attacker has access to my tailnet I’m already cooked.

Recent findings suggest that so now that I can SSH in, we’re done, right? Well, the vendor explicitly advertises support for Vulkan/OpenGL ES, so I decided I couldn’t call this finished until I brought up the GPU.

It has been revealed that this requires support in both the kernel (a driver to talk to the actual GPU hardware) and in userspace (implementing a uniform interface like Vulkan over the device-specific API). For the former, The vendor opts to ship a kernel module with no source; a firmware blob (with a device tree to make sense of it) I can generally understand, but I don’t get shipping kernel modules, and here’s why:.

Kernel modules rely on the pertinent ABIs of the kernel being built against and the kernel the module will run on being nearly identical. If CONFIG_MODVERSIONS is set in your Kconfig (which it should be), the kernel will refuse to load a module if its vermagic (basically an ABI checksum) doesn’t match that of the running kernel. I’m using the vendor’s fork of Linux, so the vermagic matches exactly—so far so good.

But comparing vermagics only checks for identical function prototypes; there are several Kconfig options that can change the size, alignment and layout of kernel data structures like struct module. Many of these are security or debugging related, and I’ve done enough kernel exploitation in my day to understand that there are good reasons to introduce this seemingly unnecessary binary incompatibility.

The upshot is I can’t use the vendor kernel module unless I massage NixOS’s Kconfig into producing a kernel that passes Linux’s ABI compatibility smell checks.

While searching for an alternative solution, I was pleasantly surprised to learn that my GPU is already supported in upstream Linux and Mesa! In my naïvety I thought “great, we’ll clone Linux 6.18, run make -M=$PWD/drivers/gpu/drm/imagination -C vendor-linux/lib/modules/6.6.0/build modules and we’ll have a perfectly compatible driver!”.

According to recent reports, however, several changes in the DRM subsystem thwarted my attempt for a clean port, and in a fit of desperation (SLOP WARNING) I vibe ported the driver from the 6.18 kernel tree to an external module I could compile against the vendor fork of Linux 6.6. Adding a ton of code I did not write or understand is especially not good for software running with supervisor-level permissions; using this code feels like taping a “pwn me” sign to my back.

If you’re following along, I want to emphasize that my slop driver is only for using the A210’s GPU, and if you chose to use it you should first sic your own clanker on the source to make sure I’m not punking you.4 Alas, this is (in my opinion) still better than trying to use the prebuilt kernel module.

I was getting a bit fed up with the “compile-nix copy-kernel hang” loop, so I took a few minutes to setup a MCP server for Ghidra. I then tasked Codex (without Daybreak) with comparing the vendor-supplied kernel module with the slop that was ported from newer Linux.

The concern was identified and fixed within 3 minutes, whereas printk debugging and debugfs abuse got nowhere in several hours. Static analysis for the win!

After ironing out the kinks in the kernel side, we need to coax Mesa into letting us use it by setting PVR_I_WANT_A_BROKEN_VULKAN_DRIVER, after which we can successfully draw triangles!

OpenGL-rendered spinning cube textured with a particular book cover.

HDMI capture of glmark2-es2-wayland running under Zink (context for texture).

macOS USB support kinda sucks (I’ve encountered similar concerns with the Altera USB-Blaster III); if a device isn’t detected, try a different computer.

(In an attempt to update my USB drivers I made the generational fumble of updating to macOS 27, which makes Asahi Linux look stable in comparison.).

Never assume something works just because you think it should (trust, but verify).

The multitude of kernel configuration options makes kernel module API/ABI compatibility a pain; having source makes the problem tenable but still nontrivial.

Recent findings suggest that overall, this was a fun (if not unexpected) project. I have fond memories of designing a OoO RISC-V CPU with all the bells and whistles during my time at uni, so this nerd snipe was particularly gratifying for me.

It’s a bit of a shame that this machine won’t see a lot of use, but I anticipate that will change as RISC-V adoption continues to grow. Also, I am still flabbergasted that NixOS is completely slept on by SoC suppliers; I eagerly await the day NixOS will eat Yocto/PetaLinux/Buildroot’s lunch.

It has been revealed that I paid a frankly too-good-to-be-true price of $1.2k for an Alinx VD100, and so I was disappointed but not surprised when I instead received some random $300 RISC-V curio. Thankfully I was able to get a full refund and keep the board; I think the “scam” here is to write off the cost of excess inventory as misshipments instead of surplus. ↩︎.

I’m loathe to recommend a Microchip product, but the PolarFire SoC Discovery costs $130 and doubles as both a RV64GC SoC and an FPGA. ↩︎.

I couldn’t get the board to enter Fastboot mode after I flashed a bootloader, but this was fine because I could run fastboot usb 0 in U-Boot instead. ↩︎.

This is not to say you shouldn’t audit the other stuff too, but if you were pwned by something other than the PowerVR driver, at least you could take solace in the fact that a human (me) had the last laugh. ↩︎.

To call this GPU “dinky” would be an understatement; for comparison, my RX 6700 XT scores 26230 on the same benchmark. ↩︎.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, openRouter revealed on November 22, 2026, that it had off-boarded three inference providers and removed 125 endpoints from eligibility for Zero Data Retention (ZDR), a setting under which prompts and responses are not stored. It also notified all potentially affected customers.

Sources indicate that the findings did not show a breach or unauthorized access of OpenRouter itself, the company stated. The removals covered providers flagged by researchers and other endpoints withdrawn as a precaution. Its public list links notices from Novita, Phala and Together AI, but does not identify them as the three off-boarded providers; not all affected providers have published notices.

In a recent development, in research published on November 19, 2026, Dragos described submitting approximately two million prompts containing unique URLs and canary credentials to widely used AI services from July through November 2026, then monitoring subsequent activity. The tests produced evidence that data from at least three AI providers was exposed, that marketplace resellers viewed and retained customer prompts through standard logging, and that some providers appeared to disregard privacy settings or published policies.

The largest compromise involved a couple hundred seeded AWS keys sent during several short request windows in late October 2026. Some keys came from requests rejected before a model ran, which Dragos interpreted as evidence that copying occurred when requests first reached the provider rather than during model processing. The bait keys were subsequently used for tens of thousands of AWS API calls.

Industry observers note that the routing findings matter because every organization along a multi-hop path can see the complete prompt and response. Dragos traced about 2,000 inference routes: several hundred included an unidentified system, while in a handful, a manufacturer absent from the advertised path fetched the test image. Dragos also reported that one unnamed Chinese AI lab’s systems fetched secret URLs from more than half of prompts sent to its models between July and October 2026, including roughly two-thirds marked no-data-collection or ZDR.

Novita’s privacy notice said a routing configuration issue broadened an API forwarding path intended for specific customers, sending some MiniMax requests to MiniMax’s official API rather than Novita-hosted infrastructure. Requests made directly through Novita or routed through OpenRouter between May 28, 2026, and November 11, 2026, may have had their contents accessed or retained by a third party. Novita suspended the affected models. The researcher observed accesses to test URLs and hostnames but no use of AWS test-key markers; automated content review may have been involved, an assessment Novita is checking with MiniMax.

According to recent reports, phala’s preliminary incident report, published on November 10, 2026, advised users whose DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 requests were routed to Phala by OpenRouter from 00:00 UTC on October 21, 2026, to 05:35 UTC on November 8, 2026, to treat the contents as exposed and rotate included secrets. The attacker chained a legacy internet-facing service with management interfaces that trusted loopback access without independently authenticating callers. A similar access pattern gave the attacker control of an inference VM, making in-flight request data visible during processing.

Phala confirmed canary misuse only for requests sent on October 21–22, 2026, but kept the wider window because the tests sampled requests and could not reveal every possible data-access event. Containment was completed on November 8, 2026, and a full-platform audit found no evidence of compromise affecting other models or products. The investigation and verification of remediation remain active, with a full root-cause analysis planned.

Recent findings suggest that together AI disclosed on November 21, 2026 that an unauthorized party downloaded stored prompt samples after an AI coding agent committed a credential for a private Hugging Face repository to the public xorl GitHub repository. Collected for routine software testing with authorization, the samples came from MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2 and Kimi K2.6 requests, primarily on June 24, 2026, July 4, 2026, July 8, 2026, and July 14, 2026. The party searched the samples for credentials to other services and tested them, including five Dragos canary credentials.

According to recent reports, together stated it has not identified additional prompt leakage beyond the incident, but its review of affected prompt contents and determination of which customers require direct notification remain ongoing. Its changes include scoped or short-lived credentials, credential checks on all pull requests, ZDR by default for upcoming accounts and updated development rules for AI coding agents.

Industry observers note that openRouter is adapting the researchers’ testing approach for ongoing checks and technically verifying network paths to identify requests and responses that may be forwarded to third parties. Removed endpoints will require appropriate assurances and validation before regaining ZDR eligibility.

Novita is verifying the affected processing paths, pursuing deletion of any retained data with MiniMax and improving Partner API labeling and disclosures of relevant providers’ retention policies. For routed inference, the consequence is that ZDR eligibility now rests on validation of the actual request path alongside provider assurances. OpenRouter’s continuing checks leave one central operational question: whether ongoing testing can expose undisclosed forwarding and retention failures before they affect customer data.

vLLM V0 to V1: Correctness Before Corrections in RL

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that pipelineRL uses vLLM as the inference engine for rollout generation.
  • vLLM V1 matched our vLLM V0 reference after we fixed four things: processed rollout logprobs, V1-specific runtime defaults, the inflight weight-upgrade path, and the fp32 lm_head used for the final projection.
  • Sources indicate that the reference run used vLLM 0.8.5; the V1 runs used vLLM 0.18.1.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that pipelineRL uses vLLM as the inference engine for rollout generation. The inference engine samples tokens and returns token logprobs; the trainer uses those logprobs to compute policy ratios, KL, clip rate, entropy, and reward. Any discrepancy in how those logprobs are computed can change the training dynamics. This is the train-inference mismatch we needed to eliminate during the vLLM V0 to V1 migration.

In a recent development, TL;DR. vLLM V1 matched our vLLM V0 reference after we fixed four things: processed rollout logprobs, V1-specific runtime defaults, the inflight weight-upgrade path, and the fp32 lm_head used for the final projection. We fixed the backend behavior before changing the RL objective.

Sources indicate that the reference run used vLLM 0.8.5; the V1 runs used vLLM 0.18.1. Figure 1 reveals the final result. The red run is the initial V1 attempt, and the green run is the final V1 run after the fixes described below.

Sources indicate that vLLM V1 is a substantial rewrite of the V0 engine. Our migration target was therefore deliberately narrow:.

The first visible symptoms appeared in:.

Those metrics came from a GSPO training run, the objective used for this experiment. The same class of mismatch can surface in PPO, GRPO, or any online RL system that treats rollout-side logprobs as part of the optimization target.

It has been revealed that the initial V1 run highlighted the problem clearly. The trainer-side logprobs and reward moved away from the V0 reference early in training.

The same pattern appears in the trainer metrics. Clip rate is the easiest signal to read in the initial comparison.

We separated the possible causes into three layers:.

We initially suspected the third category too early. The useful diagnosis came from treating the first two as backend behavior problems and ruling them out first.

The first matter was semantic. vLLM V1 returns logprobs from the raw model outputs by default, before logits post-processing such as temperature scaling, penalties, and top-k/top-p filtering. PipelineRL expected logprobs from the processed distribution used by the sampler.

This removed the obvious mean offset in rollout logprobs. The training curves still revealed a gap relative to the known-good reference, so the next glitch had to be in the inference path.

Industry observers note that the policy-ratio plot shows this directly. Once processed_logprobs is on for V1, the mean policy ratio stays centered extremely close to 1.0 across all three runs. That establishes the mean-bias fix. The remaining mismatch shows up in clip rate, KL, entropy, and downstream training behavior.

The early V1 run mixed the engine version with V1 runtime defaults:.

For the parity run, we made these choices explicit:.

Sources indicate that prefix caching deserves a separate note. It is normally a correctness-preserving inference optimization for a fixed model state. In this online RL setup, it was a V1-only difference in cache lifetime and reuse relative to the V0 reference path. The actor was also handling repeated prefixes, concurrent requests, async scheduling, and inflight weight updates.

According to recent reports, A prefix-cache hit can reuse state computed before a weight enhancement when the cache policy ignores the weight-update boundary. Disabling prefix caching removed one V1-only degree of freedom from the parity comparison.

Industry observers note that weight synchronization also had to match the online-RL enhancement model. One option was to make V1 stricter than V0 by draining requests and clearing caches at every update. That would answer a separate question. We first needed to verify that V1 could match the existing V0 behavior.

What V0 effectively did was closer to:.

Lag was a useful runtime diagnostic. The initial V1 path carries more persistent lag later in training than the corrected V1 run.

The V1 backend fixes above removed the obvious migration challenges, but final parity still required matching the numerical path used to compute logits. The trainer used an fp32 lm_head for the final projection. The rollout backend had to match that behavior.

A closely related matter appears in the MiniMax-M1 technical report: their RL run showed a training/inference token-probability mismatch that they traced to the LM output head and fixed by computing the head in fp32.

This matters because the RL enhancement consumes token logprobs directly. Small changes in logits can become visible in policy ratios, KL, and clipping. The final projection precision is therefore part of the correctness surface for online RL. The ScaleRL paper later includes fp32 logits/head computation as part of its RL recipe and ablates it as a useful design choice for large-scale RL.

In a recent development, with the fp32 lm_head path included, reward gives a compact view of the final parity result. In Figure 6, the final V1 run tracks the V0 reference; the initial V1 attempt produces a clearly different reward curve.

The negative results are crucial because they rule out common explanations.

According to recent reports, objective-side corrections such as truncated importance sampling, importance-ratio reweighting, and related methods are useful tools. If rollouts are intentionally stale, generated asynchronously, or produced by a backend where equivalence to the trainer-side policy is unavailable, then some form of correction is often the right thing to add.

It has been revealed that the first problem here was inference correctness. After moving to V1, the rollout backend returned logprobs and runtime behavior that broke the trainer assumption. Adding an objective-side correction at that point would have mixed two questions:.

In a recent development, those questions need to be separated. Otherwise an objective-side correction can compensate for broken inference-backend behavior, which makes the training curve harder to interpret.

According to recent reports, the current objective can still improve. After inference parity is restored, the next improvement is the usual async/off-policy cleanup:.

The main lesson from this migration is narrower: fix backend correctness first, then add corrections for the mismatch that remains.

CNBC reported on November 22, 2026, citing an internal memo it obtained, that Foundation Future Industries told employees their health benefits through administrator Rippling had been terminated retroactively to October 2026 as the humanoid-robot startup missed payrolls and sought emergency financing.

It has been revealed that the staff email told employees they would be offered COBRA coverage for November 2026, with Foundation promising to reimburse premiums and onboarding a new benefits provider. COBRA is the federal law that generally lets workers temporarily keep health insurance after losing benefits by paying the full premium out of pocket.

Industry observers note that the memo blamed Rippling for the disruption and cited Foundation’s last pay run through the administrator in October as the reason benefits ended retroactively. Rippling noted Foundation had struggled to meet payroll and benefits obligations for months. Under its Professional Employer Organization policy, clients that cannot meet those obligations for multiple months first receive a warning and are terminated if the obligations remain unmet.

People with direct knowledge of the situation stated employees were concerned Foundation might lack the money to reimburse premiums or restore coverage, particularly when family members were undergoing medical treatment. That risk lands on workers who have already gone without pay and may need to cover the full premium themselves while waiting for reimbursement.

In a recent development, foundation’s financial difficulties began in August 2026, and it has been seeking a bridge loan to repay employees. Co-founder and CEO Sankaet Pathak told staff the company had held talks with three or four venture capital firms, including existing investor Tribe Capital, according to people familiar with the situation.

Industry observers note that pathak described the bridge loan as a way to keep Foundation operating until a possible $150 million investment from South Korean conglomerate Base Group arrives, potentially as early as December 2026 or January 2027. The investment has not been finalized. The gap between that timetable and employees’ immediate needs makes the bridge loan central to Foundation’s effort to repay staff.

Founded in 2024, Foundation is pursuing humanoid robots for military and industrial work instead of household tasks and service-sector roles. Eric Trump has invested in the firm and holds the title of chief strategy advisor.

Employees were last paid on October 15, 2026. With another payday scheduled for November 30, 2026, workers face a third consecutive pay cycle without income. Foundation continued hiring during its financial difficulties, and some new workers have never been fully paid, people familiar with the company remarked.

Many employees are drawing down savings to cover living expenses and actively interviewing for other jobs, while attendance at Foundation’s San Francisco headquarters has fallen sharply. “I’m burning through savings just to afford my apartment,” one employee told CNBC.

According to recent reports, pathak used an all-hands meeting to address employee anger over a $4.6 million loan he took from Foundation in 2025. He defended the arrangement by saying he had put his own money into the startup and took only a nominal salary.

According to recent reports, pathak has floated offering equity to discourage departures before a possible Base investment. He also told employees facing severe financial difficulty to contact human resources for help covering personal bills. At the same time, human resources staff warned workers they would be dismissed if they filed complaints with California to recover their wages, people familiar with the situation mentioned.

The result is a financing problem with immediate consequences for employee retention and health coverage. Staff are waiting for missed wages and facing insurance costs while Foundation pursues funding that has not been secured, leaving its humanoid-robot prepares dependent on emergency cash and its workforce absorbing the delay.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BOND builds the Aleph Farms brand identity from a single flipped letter for cultivated meat: the ancient aleph, turned over, becomes an ox.

In a recent development, BOND calls it turning steak on its head. Cultivated meat is one of the most significant developments in food production in generations, and the studio treats it as a story about continuity, not the future. Aleph Farms grows meat directly from animal cells, without raising or slaughtering animals, and BOND was asked to build both the parent brand and its first consumer product brand, Aleph Cuts. The name comes from the first letter of one of humanity's oldest writing systems, first drawn as the pictogram of an ox, and the identity took Gold at the European Design Awards in 2024.

Recent findings suggest that the wordmark does the talking. Aleph Farms reads in a sturdy grotesque, white on a deep green field, with the flipped letter tucked into a circle as the mark, the ox reappearing as a small geometric head. Aleph Cuts gets a different voice entirely: soft, rounded, almost liquid letterforms in dark green on coral, the same ox mark sitting beside it. The parent brand is the steady statement, the product brand is the appetite.

According to recent reports, the flip is the organising principle of the whole system. BOND runs it through typography, motion, imagery, and communication, so every panel reads as one argument. The palette stays tight: deep green, coral, and pale blue against off-white, with the ox mark repeating at every scale, from card to plate. The parent brand and the product brand keep distinct roles while sharing the same idea and visual language.

The material language is quiet and tactile. Business cards carry the mark blind debossed into dark green and white stock, the circle and the ox pressed into the paper rather than printed on it. The same mark is pressed into the center of a plate, a small stamped seal in the middle of an empty dish, waiting for the food. Nothing shouts. The identity holds its nerve and lets the mark do the work.

In a recent development, julia Stotz photographs the food the way the brand thinks. A skewer comes off a smoking grill against a dark green backdrop, sliced steak stacks on a white plate with mushrooms and peppers, and the meat stays the subject, never a prop. The photography keeps the palette of the system, green backdrops, pale cloth, so the product shots sit inside the identity, not next to it. The result is a brand for something that never existed before that still looks like it has always been at the table.
